section.title: The Prayer of Faith
section.sectionRationale: The letter closes as it has run throughout, calling faith into action, now in the practice of prayer and the recovery of the straying. James commands prayer in every circumstance, directs the sick to the elders, promises much from the prayer of faith, holds up Elijah as proof that ordinary people's prayers move heaven, and ends with the great work of turning a wanderer back to the truth. There is no formal farewell; the last word is a rescued soul.
section.thesis: Prayer is the fitting response to every season of life, and the believing, righteous prayer of God's people, offered together and even for the straying, has real power to heal, to forgive, and to save a soul from death.
section.frameNote: Three movements: prayer for every circumstance and for the sick; the powerful prayer of the righteous, proven by Elijah; and the saving work of restoring a wanderer.

units.label: Prayer for every season
units.note: the sick, the elders, and the oil

verses.text: Is any one of you suffering? He should {{proseuchomai|pray}}. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises.
Is any one of you sick? He should call the {{presbyteroi|elders}} of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.
And the {{euche|prayer offered in faith}} will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven.

units.label: The powerful prayer of the righteous
units.note: Elijah, a man just like us

verses.text: Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a {{dikaios|righteous man}} has great power to prevail.
Elijah was a man just like us. He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain on the land for three and a half years.
Again he prayed, and the heavens gave rain, and the earth yielded its crops.
My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back,
consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.

proseuchomai.gloss: To pray, to address God in petition and worship. James makes prayer the natural response to every condition: the suffering pray, the cheerful sing praise, the sick call for prayer. Prayer runs through the whole passage as the lifeline of faith in every season.

presbyteroi.gloss: Elders, the recognized spiritual leaders of a local church. The sick are to call them to pray and anoint with oil in the Lord's name, showing that healing is sought through the ministry of the church, not a lone healer. The elders act as shepherds interceding for the flock.

euche.gloss: A prayer or vow; here the prayer offered in faith that restores the sick. James stresses that it is faith, not the ritual, that God honors, and that the Lord Himself raises the person up. The confidence rests on God's power and will, not on a technique.

dikaios.gloss: Righteous, upright, right with God. The prayer of a righteous person has great power in its working. Elijah is offered as proof: a man of like nature to us whose earnest, righteous prayer shut and opened the heavens. Righteousness here is not sinless perfection but a life rightly related to God through faith.

basic.context: James ends by weaving everything back to prayer. Whatever your situation, pray: if you are suffering, pray; if you are glad, sing; if you are sick, call the church's elders to pray over you and anoint you with oil in the Lord's name. He promises that the prayer of faith will restore the sick, that the Lord will raise them up, and that sins will be forgiven. So confess your sins to each other and pray for each other. To prove that ordinary prayers matter, he points to Elijah, a man just like us, whose prayers stopped and started the rain. And he closes with a call to go after those who wander from the truth, because bringing a straying sinner back saves a soul from death.
basic.hermeneutics: This is intensely practical, prescriptive teaching about the life of prayer in the church. The main interpretive care concerns verses 14 to 15 on healing: James promises much from the prayer of faith, yet the whole Bible, and James himself with his stress on patient suffering, keeps this within God's sovereign will. The anointing with oil is done in the name of the Lord as an act of consecrated prayer, not magic. The closing verses show that James cares supremely about the eternal rescue of the soul, not only physical restoration.
basic.originalLanguages: The passage is stitched together by proseuchomai, to pray, the response to every season. The sick call the presbyteroi, the elders. It is the euche, the prayer of faith, that restores, God honoring faith rather than ritual. And the prayer of the dikaios, the righteous person, has great power, proven by Elijah.
basic.typology: The anointing with oil in the Lord's name connects to the Spirit and to Christ, the Anointed One, in whose name the church prays. Elijah, whose prayer shut and opened the heavens, foreshadows the greater intercession of Christ and the power of prayer in His name. Saving a soul from death and covering a multitude of sins points to the atoning, restoring work of Christ, in whom sins are truly covered.
basic.christ: Everything here is done in the name of the Lord, that is, in the name of Jesus, through whom the church prays and is heard. Christ is the great intercessor whose prayers never fail, and He is the Savior whose blood covers the multitude of sins that turning a wanderer back brings under His mercy. The One who raises up the sick is the risen Lord who will finally raise all His people.
basic.god: God is the hearer and answerer of prayer in every circumstance, the Lord who raises up the sick and forgives sin. He honors the faith-filled prayer of ordinary righteous people, as He did Elijah's. He is compassionate toward the straying and delights when a sinner is turned back, for He is the God who saves souls from death. Prayer works because He is powerful, present, and merciful.
basic.crossReferences: Elijah's prayers about the rain are recorded in 1 Kings 17 to 18. Jesus taught persistent, believing prayer, Matthew 7:7-11 and Mark 11:24. Covering a multitude of sins echoes Proverbs 10:12 and 1 Peter 4:8. And Galatians 6:1 speaks of gently restoring one caught in sin.
basic.oneStory: From Elijah on Carmel to the praying church, God has always acted through the prayers of His people and pursued the wanderer to bring him home. James ends the letter not with a farewell but with a rescued soul, drawing together its great theme: faith that lives, prays, and loves. All of it is in the name of the Lord Jesus, the intercessor and Savior who raises the sick, forgives sin, and covers a multitude of transgressions, and who is bringing many wandering souls back to the truth.

context.literary:
The closing paragraph is held together by one word family. Prayer vocabulary appears in every verse from 13 to 18, and then, remarkably, it disappears in verses 19 and 20, replaced by the action that prayer exists to serve. The structure is a widening circle. It begins with the single believer asking what to do in suffering or gladness, moves to the sick person and the gathered elders, widens to the whole community confessing and praying 'for each other,' reaches back to Elijah in the history of Israel, and ends with someone going after a person who has drifted.

The opening is a run of short questions, each with its answer: 'Is any one of you suffering? ... Is anyone cheerful? ... Is any one of you sick?' James is working like a pastor with a list of cases. The answers are all imperatives, and each is short.

There are also echoes of the beginning of the letter. The salvation of the soul appears at 1:21, where the planted word 'can save your souls,' and again at 5:20, where the one who turns a sinner back 'will save his soul from death.' The address 'my brothers' opens the letter at 1:2 and closes it here. Prayer for wisdom was commended at 1:5, and the prayer that does not doubt at 1:6, and now these themes come to rest in a community that prays together. Truth is the word's own name at 1:18, and in verse 19 it is what a person can wander from.

The letter closes without a farewell or greeting, which is unusual for an ancient letter. The last picture is a rescued person.
context.historical:
Elders were the ordinary leaders of a local congregation in the first century, and the practice of appointing several in each church is attested in Acts 14:23 and Titus 1:5. They were the shepherds of the flock, 1 Peter 5:1 to 4, so it was natural for the sick to look to them. James notes that the sick person is to call them, not that they are to arrive uninvited, and that there are several of them, which makes the prayer a public act of the church and not the private power of one man.

Oil had two common uses in the world James knew. It was an everyday medicine, soothing and cleansing wounds, as the Samaritan used it on the injured man in Luke 10:34 and as Isaiah 1:6 describes a wound 'neither cleansed nor bandaged nor soothed with oil.' It was also a sign of being set apart for God, as kings and priests were anointed. Mark 6:13 reports that the Twelve anointed many sick people with oil and healed them. James says it is applied 'in the name of the Lord,' which makes it more than medicine.

Sickness was commonly seen as linked to sin in the ancient world, and the Bible sometimes confirms the connection, 1 Corinthians 11:30 for one, and sometimes denies it, as in the book of Job. James's careful 'if he has sinned' leaves room for both.

Elijah was a household name. Later Jewish writing such as Sirach 48 remembers him as the one who shut up the heavens, and Malachi 4:5 promised his return before the Day of the LORD. James says he was a man 'just like us' to show that no special class of person is needed. The three and a half years of drought is not stated in the Old Testament narrative, but Jesus uses the same figure in Luke 4:25, which shows it was a well known tradition.
context.canonical:
The prayer of the righteous has a long history behind it. Elijah's story is in 1 Kings 17 and 18. He announces the drought in 1 Kings 17:1, and the account of the rain in 1 Kings 18:42 to 45 shows him with his face between his knees while his servant looks seven times toward the sea. Jesus recalls the same drought in Luke 4:25, and Revelation 11:6 gives the two witnesses the same power to shut the sky.

The link between sickness, sin and forgiveness runs through the Psalms. David says in Psalm 32:1 to 5 that his body wasted until he confessed, and Psalm 103:3 gives the Lord as the one 'who forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.' Hezekiah's prayer in 2 Kings 20:1 to 7 is the classic case of a sick man whose prayer changes the outcome.

In the Gospels Jesus joins healing and forgiveness in one act in Mark 2:5 to 12. The apostolic church carries on the practice of healing in the Lord's name, Acts 3:6, and teaches that confessing sin brings forgiveness, 1 John 1:9.

The closing verse draws on Proverbs 10:12, 'love covers all transgressions,' which Peter also quotes in 1 Peter 4:8, and on Psalm 32:1, 'whose sins are covered,' which Paul uses of justification in Romans 4:7. Galatians 6:1 asks the spiritual to restore the one caught in sin with gentleness, and Jude 22 and 23 tells believers to show mercy to doubters and to snatch others from the fire.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
James wanted his readers to leave the letter praying. Throughout the book he has demanded faith that works, and the last chapter shows what that looks like in a community under pressure. Whatever state a person is in, whether in pain, in joy or in illness, there is one fitting response, and it is not complaining and not self reliance.

He also wanted the church to stop treating illness as an individual's private burden. The sick person is to summon the elders, and the whole congregation is to confess and pray for one another. A church that does this is a church where nobody has to hide a weakness or a fault.

Verses 17 and 18 are there to answer an unspoken objection. Readers might think that great prayers belong to great men. James answers that Elijah shared our nature, and what made his prayer powerful was the God he was asking, not the man.

Finally, the letter ends with the most serious matter. A believer who strays is in danger, and bringing him back is among the most important things a church does. James wanted the first hearers to take the wandering brother or sister seriously enough to go after them, and to take courage from the promise that such work saves a person and covers sins.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The commands are plain: pray, sing, call the elders, confess, pray for one another, and go after the wanderer. They are instructions for the church in every age. The promises attached, that the prayer of faith will restore and that the Lord will raise up, are given as the expected result of obedience, but James does not describe particular healings and does not say how quickly or in what form God answers.

What is described and not commanded is Elijah's story. His prayers shut and opened the sky once, in a unique moment of Israel's history. James does not tell the church to pray for droughts. He holds it up to show that the same kind of person with the same kind of prayer can be heard. The application is encouragement, not a pattern to copy.

The guard against misuse is the rest of Scripture. Paul asked three times for his thorn to be removed and was told that grace was sufficient, 2 Corinthians 12:8 and 9. Trophimus was left sick at Miletus, 2 Timothy 4:20, and Epaphroditus nearly died before God had mercy on him, Philippians 2:27. These accounts do not cancel James's promise. They show that prayer for healing is always offered to a God who answers as He sees best, and that a sickness that continues is not proof that anyone's faith was lacking.

debates.question: What does the anointing with oil signify?

views.label: A medicinal act joined to prayer
views.case: Oil was an everyday remedy, Luke 10:34 and Isaiah 1:6, so James would be telling the church to give the best care available and to pray at the same time. Some interpreters, Protestant ones especially, have leaned on this reading, since it avoids a sacramental use of oil. The weakness is that the phrase 'in the name of the Lord' seems to give the act a spiritual meaning beyond care.

views.label: A symbolic act of setting apart
views.case: The oil stands for consecration and for the Spirit, marking the sick person as brought before God. Mark 6:13 shows the Twelve using it together with healing. Many evangelical and charismatic churches practise it this way, as an outward sign of faith that is not itself the cure.

views.label: A sacrament of the church
views.case: The Catholic Church has long taught that the anointing of the sick is a sacrament instituted by Christ and made known by James. In earlier centuries it came to be used mainly for the dying, and since the Second Vatican Council it is offered more widely to the seriously ill. Protestants reply that the text asks for the sick to be restored, not prepared for death, and that no church office is described as holding sacramental power.

debates.bearing: All three views take the practice seriously and agree that the oil does no work on its own. The healing is attributed to the prayer and to the Lord who raises up.

debates.question: Does the prayer of faith always heal?

views.label: Yes, if the faith is real
views.case: The promise reads without condition: the prayer offered in faith will restore the sick person. Those who hold this view, including many in the faith healing tradition, argue that continuing sickness points to a lack of faith or hidden sin, and they take James 1:6 as the pattern.

views.label: Only as God wills
views.case: The great majority of interpreters hold that James's promise must be read with 1 John 5:14, 'if we ask anything according to His will, He hears us,' and with the cases of Paul, Trophimus and Epaphroditus. The prayer is genuine and often answered, but the faith it expresses is trust in God and not a technique for forcing His hand.

views.label: Mainly spiritual restoration
views.case: Some argue that the word for the sick person in verse 15 means someone worn out, and that the verb translated 'restore' is the ordinary verb for saving, so the passage speaks of a discouraged or spiritually failing believer who is restored. Others reply that verse 14 names a literal sickness and verse 15 joins it to forgiveness, so both are in view.

debates.bearing: What every reading shares is that a church is told to pray for its sick, expect God to hear, and leave the result in His hands without blaming the sufferer.

study.originalLanguages:
The first notable word is how James names the sick. In verse 14 the sick person is the one who 'is sick,' asthenei, from the word for weakness. In verse 15 he is the one who is 'sick' again in the BSB, but the Greek there is a different verb, kamno, which means to be worn out or weary. Hebrews 12:3 uses it of growing weary and losing heart. The two terms together give the picture of a person who is both physically ill and drained, and they leave open the possibility that the strain is partly spiritual.

The verb for the anointing is aleipho, the common word for rubbing on oil, as in Mark 6:13. It is not chrio, the verb Luke 4:18 uses for Christ being anointed by the Spirit. James therefore is not describing a consecration of a king or priest. He is describing the everyday act of applying oil and giving it new meaning by doing it 'in the name of the Lord.'

The word translated 'restore' in verse 15 is sozo, the great verb of salvation, and it appears again in verse 20, 'save his soul from death.' The Greek verb often means rescue from physical danger and from spiritual loss, and James plays on both. The verb for 'raise up,' egeiro, is the verb used for raising from bed and also for resurrection, so the promise carries an overtone beyond the sickroom.

In verse 16 the verb for 'healed,' iaomai, is again used for both physical and spiritual healing. Peter says that 'by His stripes you are healed,' 1 Peter 2:24, where the meaning is spiritual. The confession James asks for, exomologeo, is a public acknowledgement 'to each other,' the same verb used of people confessing sins to John in the Jordan, Matthew 3:6.

The phrase 'great power to prevail' translates polu ischuei plus the participle energoumene. The participle can mean 'when it is at work' or 'when it is earnest,' and translators are divided. Either way, the prayer is the sort that is active and not merely recited. The word for the petition here is deesis, a request made from need, set beside euche in verse 15.

Elijah 'was a man just like us,' homoiopathes, which means of like nature and feeling. Paul and Barnabas use the same word in Acts 14:15 to refuse worship. 'He prayed earnestly' is literally 'he prayed with prayer,' a Semitic way of stressing intensity.

Finally the wanderer in verse 19 'wanders,' planao, the verb for going astray, and the one who turns him back uses epistrepho, to turn around, the word for conversion in Acts 3:19.

typology.type: The anointing in the name of the Lord
typology.fulfillment: Oil in the Old Testament marked kings, priests and prophets as set apart, and 'Christ' means the Anointed One. Luke 4:18 has Jesus read that the Spirit of the Lord has anointed Him, and Acts 10:38 says God anointed Him with the Holy Spirit and power, so that He went about doing good and healing. When the church anoints the sick in His name, it works from His anointing and not its own. The correspondence is real, but the oil is only a sign. It does not carry the Spirit's power by itself, and the church's anointing is borrowed from the One who holds it fully.

typology.type: Elijah and the shutting and opening of the sky
typology.fulfillment: Elijah stands for the prophet whose word stops and starts the rain. Jesus recalls him in Luke 4:25, raises a widow's son as Elijah did in 1 Kings 17:17 to 24, and is taken by some for Elijah, Mark 8:28. Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah's return, and Jesus tells His disciples that this was fulfilled in John the Baptist, Matthew 17:12 and 13. In Christ the pattern reaches its height: His word calms the wind and raises the dead. Elijah falls short because he was human, fearful and exhausted after Carmel, 1 Kings 19:4, and he needed God to answer. Christ is the answer.

typology.type: The wanderer brought back, the shepherd and the strays
typology.fulfillment: God promises through Ezekiel to seek the lost and bring back the strays, Ezekiel 34:16. Jesus enacts this in the parable of the lost sheep, Luke 15:4 to 7, where the shepherd goes after the one and carries it home rejoicing. James asks the church to share this work, and Peter calls Christ the Chief Shepherd for whom the elders act, 1 Peter 5:4. The type is partial. Human shepherds can turn a person around, but only Christ can bear the sins that have made the person stray, 1 Peter 2:24.

The language of covering comes from the sacrificial system, in which blood covers sin and the Day of Atonement ritual lays all iniquities on a goat that carries them away, Leviticus 16:21 and 22. David uses it in Psalm 32:1, 'whose sins are covered,' and Paul takes it as a word for justification, Romans 4:7. In Christ the covering is complete: His blood purifies the conscience from works of death, Hebrews 9:14. When one believer turns another back, he does not provide the covering himself. He brings the person to the place where God's covering is applied.

study.christ:
The passage never names Jesus, but it is steeped in His name. Everything is done 'in the name of the Lord,' and in the letter that Lord is Jesus Christ, 1:1 and 2:1. The church's prayer is made through Him, as He promised: 'If you ask Me for anything in My name, I will do it,' John 14:14. Peter heals the lame man in the same way, 'In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, get up and walk,' Acts 3:6. When the elders pray, they stand where Christ's own authority has been delegated to the church.

The verbs of the promise are also Christ's. 'Raise up' is the verb of resurrection, and 'forgiven' recalls the incident of Mark 2:5 to 12, where Jesus pronounces forgiveness over a paralysed man and then heals him to show that He has authority to do both. James has the same pair: the Lord raises up and forgives. The church is not inventing a ministry but sharing in the work of its risen Head.

Christ is also the praying one at the heart of the passage. If the righteous person's prayer has great power, how much more His. Hebrews 7:25 says He 'always lives to intercede' for those who come to God through Him, and Romans 8:34 says He is at the right hand of God and interceding for us. Believers pray to a Father who is already hearing the Son pray for them. The point is not that human prayer is empty but that it is caught up in His.

The final verses lead to Him as well. The wanderer is a lost sheep, and Jesus describes Himself as the shepherd who leaves the ninety nine to find it, Luke 15:4 to 7. The 'multitude of sins' that are covered is covered at the cost of His blood, 1 Peter 2:24, and the soul saved from death is saved because He tasted death for everyone, Hebrews 2:9. When James ends on a rescued person, he ends on the work that Christ came to do.

A word of care. Elijah is not a hidden picture of Christ at every point, and the oil is not a mystical channel. The links stand where the text and the New Testament place them: the name, the intercession, the shepherd and the covering.
study.god:
The passage shows a God who hears. The first and plainest claim is that prayer is the right response to every condition of life, and that is true because there is Someone listening. Suffering, cheerfulness and sickness are all brought to Him, which makes Him the Lord of both the sorrow and the song. His attention extends to small things. The prayer of a single sick person, summoned in the quiet of a home, is heard in the court of heaven.

He is the Lord who heals and forgives. Exodus 15:26 gives His name, 'the LORD who heals you,' and Psalm 103:3 praises the one who 'forgives all your iniquities and heals all your diseases.' James keeps the two together, and so does the Bible. God cares about bodies and about souls, and He does not treat the one as a side issue to the other.

He is the God who governs creation and answers within it. The rain obeyed Elijah's prayer because the God who sends rain, Deuteronomy 11:14, chose to act through it. The heavens are shut and opened by His hand, and He is pleased to use the asking of His people as one of the means. That does not make prayer a lever. 1 John 5:14 ties the confidence to His will, and 2 Corinthians 12:9 shows Him answering with grace when He does not answer with a cure.

He is also a God who pursues the wanderer. Ezekiel 33:11 says He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but wants them to turn and live. The ordinary work of one believer turning another round is His own work carried by human hands.

And He is a God who delights to use ordinary people. Elijah was 'just like us.' The power in his prayer did not come from his nature but from the God who heard him.

For worship, the passage teaches a faith that is both bold and humble. It asks boldly, because it knows He hears, and it submits, because it knows He is wiser.

crossReferences.note: Elijah announces to Ahab that there will be neither dew nor rain except at his word. This is the start of the drought James has in mind. The text does not record the prayer, and James supplies it, showing that the prophet's word was backed by earnest petition.

On Carmel Elijah bends down with his face between his knees and sends his servant seven times to look for a cloud, until a small one appears. It shows what James means by earnest prayer: persistent, humble and watchful, and answered only after repeated asking.

Jesus speaks of the sky being shut for three and a half years in Elijah's time. The Old Testament account does not state the length, so James and Luke share a well known tradition, and both treat the drought as proof that God acts in answer to His prophet.

The Twelve cast out demons and anoint many sick people with oil and heal them. It is the nearest parallel to the elders' anointing in James and shows that oil was already used alongside healing prayer in the earliest ministry of Jesus' followers.

Jesus tells a paralysed man that his sins are forgiven and then heals him, showing that He has authority to do both. James 5:15 holds the same two promises side by side, raising up the sick and forgiving sin, as the continued work of the same Lord.

David describes bones wasting away while he kept silent, then acknowledges his sin and is forgiven. It is the Old Testament background for James's link between confession and healing, and shows how hidden guilt can weigh on the body as well as the conscience.

Paul says that some in Corinth were weak and sick, and some had died, because of how they treated the Lord's table. It confirms that sickness and sin are sometimes linked, but Paul frames the discipline as the Lord's way of keeping His people from condemnation, not as cruelty.

Paul pleaded three times for his thorn to be removed and was told that grace was sufficient. This is the necessary balance to James 5:15. Prayer is real and heard, but the answer may be strength to bear a weakness rather than its removal.

John promises that God hears whatever we ask according to His will, and then speaks of praying for a brother who is sinning. The conditions he gives clarify the promise of James and also parallel the final call to pray for those who go astray.
Hatred stirs up dissension, but love covers all transgressions. James 5:20 draws on this proverb, which shows that turning someone back is an act of love that deals with sin rather than airing it.

Paul tells the spiritual to restore one caught in a trespass gently, and to carry one another's burdens. It gives the manner of the work James commends in verses 19 and 20, which is humble, wary of one's own weakness, and aimed at restoring.
God says He will seek the lost, bring back the strays and strengthen the weak. James's wanderer is one of these, and the church takes part in what the Lord has already promised to do Himself.

study.oneStory:
The Bible begins with creation as a place of open fellowship with God, and the fall brought illness, estrangement and death. This passage lives in the world after that fall and shows what the church does in it. It prays, it confesses, it cares for the sick and it goes after the lost. Each of these is a small mending of what Genesis 3 broke: the body, the conscience, the community and the relationship with God.

The Old Testament supplies the groundwork. God is the one who heals, Exodus 15:26. The prophets speak to Him with great power, as Elijah does on Carmel. The psalmists show confession bringing relief. The whole story of Israel is a story of people who wander and are sought, and the Lord's promise to seek the strays in Ezekiel 34:16 is the great statement of it.

The New Testament shows these hopes being met in Christ. He heals and forgives together, He sends His followers to anoint and pray in His name, and He intercedes for them at the Father's right hand. The church is the community He gathers and then entrusts with the work of mutual care. James is giving it shape for the long interval before He returns.

The story ends in a place where all of this is complete. In the new creation there is no more sickness, because God Himself wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and the leaves of the tree of life are for the healing of the nations, Revelation 22:2. There is no more wandering, because the Shepherd gathers His flock and none is lost. Prayer there is not asking but face to face worship. Until then, every prayer of the righteous, every confession and every rescued wanderer is a first instalment of the world to come.

quiz.q: What is James's counsel for the different seasons of life in verse 13?

options.text: The suffering should pray, and the cheerful should sing praises.
options.note: Verse 13: prayer and praise as the response to every circumstance.

options.text: Every situation should turn us toward God in prayer or praise.
options.note: True to the thrust, if less specific than the verse.

options.text: We should only pray when things are going badly.
options.note: James includes praise in good times, not prayer only in trouble.

options.text: We should handle each season on our own strength.
options.note: The whole point is to bring every season to God.

quiz.q: What does James direct the sick person to do?

options.text: Call the elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the Lord's name.
options.note: Verse 14: healing sought through the praying ministry of the church.

options.text: Seek the prayer of the church's leaders in the name of the Lord.
options.note: True to the verse, capturing the corporate, prayerful nature.

options.text: Find a single gifted healer to perform a ritual.
options.note: James points to the elders together, not a lone healer or ritual.

options.text: Keep the illness private and tell no one.
options.note: The opposite: call the elders and confess to one another.

quiz.q: How should we understand the promise that the prayer of faith restores the sick?

options.text: A real promise to pray boldly, held within God's sovereign will and including forgiveness.
options.note: The confidence rests on God's power and goodness, not a guaranteed technique.

options.text: The restoring and raising up embrace the whole person, as God wills.
options.note: True, noting the words can reach to spiritual restoration and resurrection.

options.text: A guarantee that every faithful prayer always brings physical healing.
options.note: Scripture and James's call to patient suffering qualify this; it is not a formula.

options.text: A statement that prayer for the sick is pointless.
options.note: James urges such prayer with real expectation that God acts.

quiz.q: Why does James point to Elijah in verses 17 to 18?

options.text: To show that an ordinary person's earnest, righteous prayer has great power.
options.note: Verse 17: Elijah was a man just like us, yet his prayers moved heaven.

options.text: To encourage fervent, believing prayer from those walking rightly with God.
options.note: True, linking to the righteous man's prayer in verse 16.

options.text: To prove that only unique prophets can expect answered prayer.
options.note: The stress is that Elijah was just like us, so prayer is for all.

options.text: To show that prayer is a mechanical lever that forces God's hand.
options.note: Prayer prevails because God hears, not by mechanical technique.

quiz.q: What does James say about turning a wanderer back from error?

options.text: It saves the sinner's soul from death and covers a multitude of sins.
options.note: Verse 20: restoring the straying is a soul-saving work.

options.text: Bringing back one who strays from the truth is of eternal importance.
options.note: True to the weight James gives it as the letter's closing note.

options.text: Wanderers are best left alone to sort themselves out.
options.note: James calls the church to go after and reclaim them.

options.text: Only ordained ministers may seek to restore a straying believer.
options.note: James says whoever turns a sinner back, addressing all the brothers.

questions: James makes prayer the response to every season. Do you instinctively turn to God in both suffering and joy, or only in one of them?
The sick are told to call the elders and the church to confess and pray together. What keeps you from inviting others into your struggles, and what would openness look like?
Elijah was a man just like us, yet his prayers were powerful. How does that change the way you view your own praying?
The letter ends by urging us to bring back those who wander from the truth. Is there someone drifting from Christ whom God may be calling you to pursue in love?
Looking back over the whole letter of James, which single call, on trials, speech, wealth, wisdom, or prayer, is God most pressing on you to obey?

translationNotes.note: Anoint him with oil renders a practice done in the name of the Lord; it frames the act as consecrated, prayerful ministry through the elders, not a magical rite.

Restore and raise him up can carry both physical and spiritual senses; the prayer offered in faith renders euche, stressing faith and the Lord's action rather than ritual, with forgiveness expressly included.

Has great power to prevail renders a phrase about the prayer of a righteous person being powerful in its working; the term dikaios, righteous, denotes a life rightly related to God, not sinless perfection.
